## The claim

No structural variant supported by two callers of different method classes, outside the bait-edge zone, removes or duplicates a coding exon of a gene that also carries a rare heterozygous protein-altering allele.

**Prediction if true.** The merged consensus of a read-pair and split-read caller (delly) with a local-assembly caller (dysgu), after calls within one insert-size of a bait boundary are flagged out, contains no such deletion or insertion overlapping a coding exon of such a gene.

**What would refute it.** A deletion or insertion does, and that gene becomes the lead pair; a duplication or inversion does, and the gene becomes a lead only when per-exon coverage or k-mer copy number confirms the dosage change, because short-read precision for those two types is close to a coin flip (Kosugi 2019, Table 1).

## History

| 1 | proposed | — | — |
| 2 | refuted | 0.25 | Refuted as written: two genes carry a two-method-class deletion over a coding exon while also holding a rare protein-altering heterozygous allele, and the pre-registered response is that such a gene becomes a lead. Both leads are weak and the entry says why. One of the two is a DECOY, a gene no symptom nominated, so the signal is not specific to the target set; both are among the most structurally polymorphic genes in the human genome, where a common benign deletion is the likelier reading; and the deletions are 139-1296 bp, far from removing a gene. The refutation also required fixing the artefact control before it meant anything: the first run's consensus included a 13 Mb deletion and a 40 Mb inversion in a living child, because the pre-registered bait-edge flag tested proximity to a boundary while these calls SPAN the unbaited gaps between baited islands. The span-coverage rule that catches them is a widened implementation of a control the plan named before the run, not a new threshold chosen after seeing the data, and the entry states the distinction. |
